One legitimate fear: if the CMS disappears, what governs the content?

The Gathering. An independent standards body — MIT licensed, practitioner-led, modelled on the W3C. The Gathering defines the cog specification: what metadata is required, how access is controlled, how quality is measured, how governance works. The standard is open. No fees. No gatekeeping.

MX OS is one implementation of that standard. Like Linux running on POSIX. The standard belongs to everyone. Products are built on it. If CogNovaMX disappeared tomorrow, the cogs would still work. They’re text files. Any future system that can parse YAML and read markdown can use them.

This is the opposite of vendor lock-in. It’s vendor irrelevance. Not because vendors don’t matter, but because the content doesn’t depend on any vendor to exist, to be read, or to be delivered.

What Adoption Looks Like

The remaining problem is adoption. It’s real and it’s significant.

Most content in the world today is not self-describing. It lives in databases, proprietary formats, PDF files, Word documents, and web pages without structured metadata. Converting that content to cogs — or creating new content as cogs from the start — requires a shift in practice.

The shift is smaller than it appears, however. A cog is any document with MX metadata — most commonly a markdown file with YAML frontmatter, or an HTML page with Schema.org JSON-LD and <meta name="mx:*"> tags. Most content professionals already write in markdown. Most structured content systems already use YAML or JSON for metadata. The conceptual gap between “content in a headless CMS with structured fields” and “content in a cog with structured metadata” is narrow. The difference is where it lives: on a platform, or on a filesystem.

The lift-and-shift service handles existing content. The datalake — the cog collection — absorbs what the CMS held. New content is authored as cogs from the start. The transition is not “throw everything away and start over.” It’s “migrate what you have and write new things differently.”

The Machine Experience provides the incentive. When users see the difference between a generic website and a personalised MX View generated from cog data, the value proposition becomes visceral. Site owners who adopt cog metadata get better engagement, better accessibility, and personalisation at scale without privacy liability. The business case makes itself.

The Last Line

I’ve been in content systems since 1977. I’ve watched five generations of content management solve five real problems and create five new ones. Each generation was the right answer for its moment. Each moment passed.

Cogs are the fifth generation. Content that describes itself. Files that carry their own context. Intelligence that reads them and acts. No platform required.

The CMS was the cocoon. It protected content while the web grew. It gave us authoring, workflows, delivery, and scale. It was necessary and it was good.

Now the content has its own wings. Where it goes next is up to the people who write it.

Content that describes itself doesn’t need a manager.

The evolution of content management is not a story of failure. It’s a story of each generation building the foundation for the next. The CMS professionals who built structured content systems, who championed metadata, who pushed for API-first architecture — they built the road that leads here. This chapter is written with respect for that work and honesty about where it leads.

Chapter 18 — The Information Architecture of the LLM Web

The patterns are the bricks. This chapter is the blueprint.

Every chapter in this book addresses a facet of machine comprehension — semantic HTML, structured data, navigation, metadata, convergence patterns, content management. Each facet is essential. None is sufficient alone. Information architecture is the discipline that connects them into a coherent whole — the difference between a pile of well-made bricks and a building that stands.

Traditional information architecture optimises for human wayfinding. A visitor lands on your home page, scans the navigation, clicks through to a category, finds what they need. The discipline has decades of proven principles: clear labelling, consistent navigation, shallow hierarchies, breadcrumb trails. Steve Krug’s “Don’t Make Me Think” remains the gold standard for human-centred IA.

Machine-focused IA shares the same goal — don’t make the visitor think — but the visitor thinks differently. An AI agent does not scan a navigation bar. It parses a DOM tree. It does not follow visual hierarchy. It follows semantic hierarchy. It does not browse. It traverses. The architectural decisions that make a site navigable for humans and parsable for machines are often the same decisions, but the reasons they work are different, and understanding those reasons is what separates competent implementation from architectural coherence.

This chapter names the framework that connects everything. It is the architectural expression of MX — the discipline that ensures machines can find, understand, and act on your content without guessing.

The Architectural View

The book presents machine-readable structure at three distinct scales. Chapter 10 introduces “Three Layers of Discovery” in the context of Generative Engine Optimisation — site-wide guidance, page-level metadata, and content structure. The Handbook’s chapters on navigation (Chapter 6), content architecture (Chapter 4), and how AI reads pages (Chapter 2) each address one scale in depth. What no single chapter does is name the unified model and show how the layers depend on each other.

The Three-Layer IA Framework:

  • Site layer — how agents discover and traverse your site. Sitemaps, robots.txt, llms.txt, URL hierarchy, internal linking topology, hub-and-spoke architecture, .mx.yaml.md folder metadata. This is the macro structure that determines whether agents can find your pages at all. Chapter 6 of the Handbook and Chapter 10 provide the implementation patterns.

  • Page layer — how agents parse and comprehend individual pages. Heading hierarchy, landmark roles (<main>, <nav>, <article>, <aside>), DOM ordering, breadcrumb navigation, content sections, MX meta tags (mx:type, mx:audience, mx:status), YAML frontmatter for documents in publishing pipelines. This is the meso structure that determines whether agents can understand a page once they arrive. Chapters 2 and 3 of the Handbook and Chapter 11 provide the patterns.

  • Content layer — how agents extract and use structured information within pages. Semantic HTML elements, Schema.org JSON-LD, definition lists, data tables, inline semantics (<time>, <data>, <dfn>), metadata blocks. This is the micro structure that determines whether agents can act on what they find. Chapter 4 of the Handbook and Chapter 12 provide the patterns.

These three layers form a dependency chain, not a menu of options. A site-layer failure — no sitemap, opaque URLs, orphan pages — prevents agents from discovering your pages. If they cannot discover pages, the page layer is irrelevant. A page-layer failure — broken heading hierarchy, missing landmarks, content buried in JavaScript — prevents agents from parsing the page. If they cannot parse it, the content layer is irrelevant.

The dependency runs in one direction: site enables page, page enables content. Fix from the top down. A beautifully marked-up product page with perfect Schema.org is invisible if the sitemap does not list it and no internal link points to it.

The framework applies equally to both mechanisms of agent access. Training-time crawlers — the systems that build Common Crawl datasets and feed model training — navigate via sitemaps and internal links at the site layer, parse HTML structure at the page layer, and extract knowledge at the content layer. Inference-time agents — the systems that fetch your site in real time during a user conversation — follow exactly the same path but with higher stakes, because the user is waiting for the answer. Chapter 2 of the Handbook details both mechanisms. The architectural principle is the same: structure that serves one serves both.

Figure 18.1: The Three-Layer IA Framework — a dependency chain where each layer enables the next. Site architecture determines discoverability, page architecture determines comprehension, content architecture determines actionability.

Taxonomy and Classification for Machines

Heading hierarchy, navigation menus, and breadcrumbs are the visible expressions of a deeper architectural decision: taxonomy. How you classify your content — what categories exist, how they relate, how deep they nest — determines the shape of everything else. Get the taxonomy wrong and no amount of semantic HTML can compensate.

Human-centred taxonomy design asks: “How would a customer look for this?” Machine-centred taxonomy design asks the same question, but the customer is an agent with a token budget and a crawl depth limit.

Depth and breadth

Agents allocate effort by depth. A crawler that starts at your home page and follows links has a finite budget — time, tokens, or request limits. Pages at depth 1 (one click from home) receive the most attention. Depth 2 receives less. By depth 4, discovery rates drop sharply. The practical implication: critical content should live within two to three clicks of the home page. Anything deeper risks being undiscovered, particularly by training-time crawlers building knowledge bases from Common Crawl snapshots.

This creates a tension. A shallow taxonomy (few levels, many items per level) maximises discoverability but reduces context. A deep taxonomy (many levels, few items per level) provides rich context but buries content. The resolution is the hub-and-spoke pattern described in Chapter 6 of the Handbook: hub pages at depth 1 or 2 that link to all their spokes, with spokes cross-linking to related spokes in other hubs. The hub provides breadth. The spoke provides depth. The cross-links provide lateral context.

Tag architecture

Tags and categories serve different architectural purposes, though many content systems conflate them.

Categories are hierarchical and exclusive. A product belongs to one category path: Electronics > Audio > Headphones > Over-Ear. This hierarchy appears in URLs (/electronics/audio/headphones/over-ear/), breadcrumbs, and sitemap structure. Categories define the site’s navigational skeleton.

Tags are flat and inclusive. The same headphones might be tagged wireless, noise-cancelling, bluetooth-5. Tags enable lateral discovery — “show me all wireless products across all categories” — without distorting the navigational hierarchy.

For machines, categories should be expressed as BreadcrumbList (the positional context) and CollectionPage with ItemList (the contents of a category). Tags should be expressed as keywords in page metadata or as additionalType properties in Schema.org, enabling agents to find related items without traversing the full category tree.

Faceted navigation

Faceted navigation — filtering by price, colour, size, rating — is standard in e-commerce. For machines, faceted navigation only works if the filter dimensions exist in the served HTML. A <select> element with <option> values, a <fieldset> with checkboxes, or URL parameters like ?colour=black&price=under-500 are machine-parsable. A JavaScript-only filter panel that manipulates the DOM without changing the URL or exposing state in HTML is invisible to any agent that does not execute JavaScript — which includes most training-time crawlers and many inference-time fetchers.

The principle: if a filter matters enough to build, it matters enough to render in served HTML.

The naming problem

The most common IA failure is not missing structure — it is inconsistent naming. When your navigation says “Headphones”, your breadcrumb says “Audio Accessories”, your URL says /headsets/, and your Schema.org says "name": "Ear Equipment", an agent sees four different taxonomies, not one. Confidence drops. Chapter 9 of the Handbook catalogues this as a specific anti-pattern.

One name per concept, used consistently across all expressions: navigation labels, breadcrumb text, URL slugs, Schema.org name properties, heading text, and sitemap labels. Decide the canonical name once and enforce it through templates.

The following example shows a single taxonomy expressed at all three IA layers:

<!-- Site layer: URL structure -->
<!-- /products/audio/headphones/over-ear/ -->

<!-- Page layer: breadcrumb navigation -->
<nav aria-label="Breadcrumb">
  <ol itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/BreadcrumbList">
    <li itemprop="itemListElement" itemscope
        itemtype="https://schema.org/ListItem">
      <a itemprop="item" href="/products/">
        <span itemprop="name">Products</span>
      </a>
      <meta itemprop="position" content="1">
    </li>
    <li itemprop="itemListElement" itemscope
        itemtype="https://schema.org/ListItem">
      <a itemprop="item" href="/products/audio/">
        <span itemprop="name">Audio</span>
      </a>
      <meta itemprop="position" content="2">
    </li>
    <li itemprop="itemListElement" itemscope
        itemtype="https://schema.org/ListItem">
      <a itemprop="item" href="/products/audio/headphones/">
        <span itemprop="name">Headphones</span>
      </a>
      <meta itemprop="position" content="3">
    </li>
    <li itemprop="itemListElement" itemscope
        itemtype="https://schema.org/ListItem">
      <span itemprop="name">Over-Ear</span>
      <meta itemprop="position" content="4">
    </li>
  </ol>
</nav>

<!-- Content layer: Schema.org classification -->
<script type="application/ld+json">
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "CollectionPage",
  "name": "Over-Ear Headphones",
  "description": "Over-ear headphones for studio, travel, and everyday use",
  "url": "https://example.com/products/audio/headphones/over-ear/",
  "breadcrumb": {
    "@type": "BreadcrumbList",
    "itemListElement": [
      { "@type": "ListItem", "position": 1, "name": "Products",
        "item": "https://example.com/products/" },
      { "@type": "ListItem", "position": 2, "name": "Audio",
        "item": "https://example.com/products/audio/" },
      { "@type": "ListItem", "position": 3, "name": "Headphones",
        "item": "https://example.com/products/audio/headphones/" },
      { "@type": "ListItem", "position": 4, "name": "Over-Ear" }
    ]
  },
  "mainEntity": {
    "@type": "ItemList",
    "numberOfItems": 24,
    "itemListElement": [
      { "@type": "Product", "name": "Studio Pro X",
        "url": "https://example.com/products/audio/headphones/over-ear/studio-pro-x" },
      { "@type": "Product", "name": "Travel Elite",
        "url": "https://example.com/products/audio/headphones/over-ear/travel-elite" }
    ]
  }
}
</script>

Notice: the names “Products”, “Audio”, “Headphones”, “Over-Ear” are identical in the URL path, the breadcrumb text, and the Schema.org name properties. One taxonomy, three expressions, zero ambiguity.

URL Design as Architecture

A URL is not a technical detail. It is the most compressed expression of your information architecture. An agent reading https://example.com/products/audio/headphones/over-ear/studio-pro-x understands five levels of classification before it fetches a single byte of HTML. An agent reading https://example.com/p?id=38291 understands nothing.

Depth limits

The practical sweet spot for URL depth is two to four path segments after the domain. This is not arbitrary — it reflects the intersection of crawl budget allocation, human readability, and taxonomic precision.

  • Depth 1 (/products/) — category landing pages. High priority in sitemaps, linked from global navigation. Maximum discoverability.
  • Depth 2 (/products/audio/) — subcategory pages. Still easily discoverable. Hub pages in a hub-and-spoke architecture.
  • Depth 3 (/products/audio/headphones/) — product category pages. The typical leaf node for browsing agents.
  • Depth 4 (/products/audio/headphones/studio-pro-x) — individual item pages. Discoverable via parent category listing and sitemap.
  • Depth 5+ — diminishing returns. Training-time crawlers may not reach this depth. Inference-time agents may allocate less confidence to deeply nested content.

Figure 18.2: Agent attention follows a decay curve by URL depth. Pages within two to four segments of the domain receive the most discovery traffic. Beyond four, discovery rates drop sharply — particularly for training-time crawlers.

Slug design

URL slugs are content descriptors. They should be lowercase, hyphen-separated, and semantically meaningful. /espresso-machines/rancilio-silvia-pro-x tells an agent the product name and category. /p/12847 tells it nothing.

Design rules:

  • Use the canonical name from your taxonomy (the same name that appears in navigation, breadcrumbs, and Schema.org)
  • Hyphenate multi-word slugs (over-ear not overear or over_ear)
  • Omit articles, prepositions, and filler (studio-pro-x not the-studio-pro-x-headphones)
  • Never include database IDs, session tokens, or CMS artefacts in slugs

Canonical strategy

Every page has one canonical URL. This is enforced through three mechanisms working together:

  1. rel="canonical" in the page’s <head> — tells agents which URL is authoritative
  2. Sitemap consistency — the URL in sitemap.xml matches the canonical URL exactly
  3. Redirect discipline — alternative URLs (with trailing slashes, without www, with query parameters) redirect to the canonical with 301 status codes, not 302

When these three signals disagree, agents lose confidence. A sitemap listing https://www.example.com/products/ while the page’s canonical tag points to https://example.com/products (without www) creates ambiguity. Resolve discrepancies at the source — pick one canonical form and enforce it everywhere.

Parameters and pagination

URL parameters create architectural choices. /products/headphones?page=2 and /products/headphones/page/2/ both work, but they behave differently for agents.

Query parameters (?page=2) are treated as variants of the same page by most crawlers. Path segments (/page/2/) are treated as distinct pages. For pagination, query parameters with rel="next" and rel="prev" link elements are the established convention. For filters that create meaningfully different content (?colour=black), path segments (/headphones/black/) may be appropriate if the filtered view is worth indexing independently.

The guiding principle: if the parameterised URL produces substantially different content that agents should discover independently, give it a path-segment URL. If it produces a variant of the same content (pagination, sorting, display preferences), use query parameters and declare the relationship with rel attributes.

Content Modelling for Machine Readability

Every content management system — whether a traditional CMS, a headless platform, or a static site generator — uses content models. A content model defines the fields, relationships, and content types that authors work with. These models are invisible to site visitors, but they determine what the published page can express.

The architectural insight is that content model design decisions made in the CMS propagate directly to machine readability in the served HTML. A CMS content type with a dedicated price field can output <data value="2030">£2,030</data>. A content type with a single body rich-text field outputs an unstructured paragraph that happens to mention a price. The first is machine-readable. The second requires inference.

Fields as semantic contracts

Each field in a content model is a semantic contract: a promise that this specific piece of information exists, is findable, and has a known type.

Content model field HTML output MX metadata equivalent Machine benefit
title (text) <h1> + <title> + Schema.org name YAML title: Unambiguous page identity
price (number + currency) <data value="2030"> + Schema.org price/priceCurrency — Extractable, comparable
publishDate (date) <time datetime="2026-03-15"> YAML created: / modified: Temporal context
category (taxonomy reference) Breadcrumb + URL path + Schema.org category YAML mx: contentType: Classification
status (lifecycle) — YAML mx: status: (active/draft/archived) Currency and trust
audience (who may use) <meta name="mx:audience"> YAML mx: audience: Access governance
body (rich text) <article> body content — Narrative, but unstructured
relatedProducts (references) Internal links + Schema.org isRelatedTo YAML mx: buildsOn: Navigation graph

The principle: every piece of information that matters to machine comprehension should be a discrete field in the content model, not embedded in a rich-text body. A field is a promise. A paragraph is a hope.

Content types as Schema.org types

Map each CMS content type to a Schema.org type. An “Article” content type outputs <article> with Article JSON-LD. A “Product” content type outputs Product JSON-LD. A “FAQ” content type outputs FAQPage with Question and Answer entries. Chapter 4 of the Handbook demonstrates the HTML output patterns for each of these content types.

This mapping should be deliberate, not incidental. When creating a content type, decide at design time which Schema.org type it corresponds to, which properties are required, and which fields supply those properties. The CMS template then enforces the mapping — making bad IA impossible rather than relying on authors to remember.

Relationships as navigation

Content relationships — “this product is related to these accessories”, “this article is part of this series”, “this FAQ belongs to this product” — are navigational signals. They tell agents how content connects.

Express relationships in HTML using established patterns:

  • isPartOf / hasPart in Schema.org for parent-child relationships (article in a series, product in a bundle)
  • relatedLink in Schema.org for lateral relationships
  • rel="next" / rel="prev" in <link> elements for sequential relationships
  • Internal <a> links within body content for contextual relationships

The content model should include explicit relationship fields — not rely on authors manually inserting links in body text.

Templates as IA enforcement

The CMS template is the enforcement mechanism for information architecture. A well-designed template guarantees that every page of a given type has correct heading hierarchy, complete Schema.org markup, consistent breadcrumbs, and proper landmark elements — regardless of what the author does or does not remember.

This is where content modelling connects to Chapter 14’s Three-Zone Architecture. Zone 2 (Curated/Validation) validates that metadata is complete and correct before publishing. Zone 3 (Serving/Published) applies templates that enforce structural consistency. The template layer transforms content model decisions into machine-readable HTML — reliably, repeatedly, and without relying on individual human diligence.

The following example shows a content model definition alongside the HTML output it produces:

# Content model: Product
fields:
  name:
    type: text
    required: true
    maps_to: [h1, schema:name, og:title, title]
  description:
    type: text
    required: true
    maps_to: [meta:description, schema:description, og:description]
  price:
    type: number
    currency: true
    required: true
    maps_to: [data:value, schema:price]
  category:
    type: taxonomy
    required: true
    maps_to: [breadcrumb, url:path, schema:category]
  image:
    type: asset
    required: true
    maps_to: [img:src, schema:image, og:image]
  relatedProducts:
    type: reference[]
    content_type: Product
    maps_to: [schema:isRelatedTo, internal:links]
<!-- Template output for a Product content type -->
<article itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/Product">
  <h1 itemprop="name">Rancilio Silvia Pro X</h1>

  <p itemprop="description">Dual-boiler espresso machine with PID
  temperature control for home baristas.</p>

  <p>Price: <data itemprop="price" value="2030"
     content="2030">£2,030</data>
  <meta itemprop="priceCurrency" content="GBP"></p>

  <img itemprop="image" src="/images/rancilio-silvia-pro-x.jpg"
       alt="Rancilio Silvia Pro X espresso machine"
       width="600" height="400">

  <section aria-label="Related products">
    <h2>Related Products</h2>
    <ul>
      <li><a href="/products/coffee/grinders/rocky-sd"
             itemprop="isRelatedTo">Rancilio Rocky SD Grinder</a></li>
      <li><a href="/products/coffee/accessories/tamper-58mm"
             itemprop="isRelatedTo">58mm Precision Tamper</a></li>
    </ul>
  </section>
</article>

The content model defines what exists. The template defines how it renders. The Schema.org markup makes it machine-actionable. None of these decisions are made by the author at publishing time — they are architectural decisions made once and enforced permanently.

Auditing IA for Machine Comprehension

Chapter 8 of the Handbook describes how to test individual pages — paste the HTML into an LLM, ask what it understands, note the gaps. That is page-level testing. IA auditing is different. It tests the architecture — the relationships, hierarchies, and navigation paths that connect pages into a coherent whole.

A site can have perfectly structured individual pages and still fail architecturally. Orphan pages that no navigation links to. Category pages with no sitemap entry. Breadcrumbs that contradict the URL structure. Navigation labels that do not match heading text. These are architectural failures, not page failures, and they require architectural testing.

The five-check audit

A practical IA audit follows five checks, each testing a different aspect of architectural coherence.

Check 1: Orphan detection. Crawl the site starting from the home page, following every internal link. Compare the set of discovered URLs to the set of URLs in sitemap.xml. Any URL in the sitemap but not reachable via links is an orphan — discoverable by crawlers that read sitemaps but invisible to crawlers that follow links. Any URL reachable via links but not in the sitemap is a sitemap gap. Both are IA failures.

Check 2: Depth analysis. For every page, record the minimum number of clicks from the home page. Visualise the distribution. If critical content — product pages, service descriptions, pricing — sits at depth 4 or beyond, agents may not find it. Chapter 6 of the Handbook’s Figure 6.1 shows the navigation efficiency comparison: structured navigation achieves 98% success in two steps; flat or hidden navigation drops to 30% over fifteen or more steps.

Check 3: Taxonomy consistency. For every page in a category, verify that the category name is identical in the navigation menu, the breadcrumb trail, the URL slug, and the Schema.org name property. Any discrepancy is a naming failure. Automated checking is straightforward — extract the breadcrumb text, the last URL path segment, the navigation label, and the Schema.org category value, and compare.

Check 4: Content gap analysis. List every category in your taxonomy. For each category, count the pages it contains. Categories with zero pages are empty nodes — they promise content that does not exist. Categories with a single page may indicate a classification error (the item is too specific for its own category) or incomplete content (the category should have more entries).

Check 5: Sitemap vs reality. Fetch every URL listed in sitemap.xml. Verify that each returns a 200 status code, that the rel="canonical" tag matches the sitemap URL, and that the page contains an <h1> element. URLs that return 301, 404, or 410 should be removed from the sitemap. URLs where the canonical does not match should be corrected. Pages without an <h1> lack a semantic identity.

Check 6: Metadata completeness. For every indexed page, verify that <title>, <meta name="description">, and Open Graph tags are present and non-empty. For pages in a governed publishing pipeline, verify that source documents carry YAML frontmatter with mx: status and mx: contentType. Missing governance metadata means the content has no declared lifecycle — machines cannot distinguish an active page from an archived one, or a product from a blog post, without inferring from context. Automated carrier metadata auditing tools can verify this at scale.

Figure 18.3: The IA audit workflow — five sequential checks that test site-level architectural coherence. Each check reveals a different class of IA failure: orphan pages, buried content, naming inconsistency, empty categories, and sitemap drift.

The LLM-as-auditor technique

The five-check audit uses automated tools. The LLM-as-auditor technique uses the machines themselves as testers — the same approach as the morning-after test described in Chapter 4 of the Handbook, applied at architectural scale.

Paste your sitemap.xml into an LLM. Ask: “Describe the structure of this website.” If the model cannot identify your main content areas, articulate the taxonomy, or explain how categories relate, your IA is unclear to machines.

Then take a representative page from each major category. Paste the served HTML (not the rendered page — the raw HTML source, as Chapter 12 explains). Ask the model: “What category does this page belong to? What related content would you expect to find? How would you navigate to the home page from here?” If the model struggles, inference-time agents will struggle in the same way.

This is not a replacement for automated checks — it is a complement. Automated checks find structural errors. LLM testing finds comprehension gaps.
