Traditional information architecture is the oldest discipline in this book and the least visible. It has no tag, no specification, no validator. You cannot install it from npm. MX begins to change that — YAML frontmatter, .mx.yaml.md sidecar files, and MX meta tags formalise architectural decisions into machine-readable metadata. But the discipline itself still lives in the decisions you make before you write a line of code — how you classify your content, how you name your categories, how deep you nest your pages, how consistently you label your navigation. These decisions determine whether machines can find your content, understand your structure, and act on your information. The patterns in this book are the implementation. The architecture is what makes them work together.

Chapter 19 — Cogs and Reginald

The web is made of pages. Documentation is made of files. The MX patterns described in this book make pages machine-readable. Pages are not the only things machines read, though. They read product manuals, API references, compliance documents, standard operating procedures, onboarding guides, configuration files, and policy documents. Every one of these can be made machine-readable using the same principle: structured metadata that eliminates guessing.

The cog format does this for documents. Reginald does it for trust and discovery. Together, they extend MX from websites to every digital asset an organisation produces.

The Document Problem

The website problem is well understood by now. Machines visit pages, struggle with ambiguous HTML, and either extract wrong information or give up. The document problem is identical but less visible.

An AI agent is asked to summarise a company’s refund policy. It finds a PDF on the website, reads the prose, and produces a summary. The summary is plausible. It is also wrong — because the PDF is three versions old, superseded by a policy update that exists as a Word document on a different server. The agent had no way to know this. Nothing in the PDF said “I am version 2.1, published in March 2025, and there is a newer version.” Nothing in the newer document said “I replace the document at this URL.” The metadata that would prevent this error does not exist.

This is not a failure of AI capability. It is a failure of document architecture. The information exists. It is not structured for machine consumption.

Consider the scale. A mid-sized organisation maintains thousands of documents — policies, procedures, technical references, training materials, product specifications. Some live in a CMS. Some live in SharePoint. Some live in Git repositories. Some live on file shares that nobody has audited in years. An AI agent navigating this landscape has no reliable way to determine: Is this document current? Who authored it? What does it replace? Who is the intended audience? What topics does it cover?

Every time a machine cannot answer these questions from metadata, it reads the entire document and guesses. Every guess costs compute. Every wrong guess costs trust.

The Cog Format

A cog is any file that carries structured MX metadata. The most familiar form is a markdown file with YAML frontmatter — structured metadata at the top, human-readable content below. The cog format is not limited to markdown, though. Every file type in a modern codebase has a carrier format for MX metadata:

  • Markdown (.md) — YAML frontmatter between --- fences
  • HTML (.html) — <meta name="mx:*"> tags in the <head>
  • JavaScript (.js) — JSDoc comments with @mx:* tags
  • CSS (.css) — comment blocks with @mx:* tags
  • Shell scripts (.sh) — YAML block in #-prefixed comments

Place MX metadata in any of these carriers, and the file becomes a cog — self-describing, machine-readable, governed by the same specification. A deploy script with @mx:status and @mx:contentType in its header comments is as much a cog as a markdown policy document with full YAML frontmatter. The carrier changes to match the file format. The semantics stay the same.

The most common form remains markdown, because it offers the richest metadata surface:

---
title: "Refund Policy"
version: "3.0"
description: Customer refund and returns policy for all product lines
author: Legal Team
created: 2025-01-15
modified: 2026-02-28

mx:
  status: published
  contentType: policy
  tags: [refund, returns, customer-service, compliance]
  audience: [humans, machines]
  replaces: refund-policy-v2
  maintainer: legal@example.com
---

# Refund Policy

[Human-readable policy content here]

The metadata is not buried in prose. It sits at the top in a format every programming language can parse. An AI agent reading this cog knows immediately: this is version 3.0 of the refund policy, it replaces version 2, it was last modified on 28 February 2026, and it is maintained by the legal team. No reading of prose required. No guessing. No hallucination.

An HTML page achieves the same thing differently. A <meta name="mx:status" content="published"> tag in the head tells a machine the page is current. A <meta name="mx:contentType" content="product"> tag tells it the page describes a product. The metadata lives in the format the file already uses. No separate sidecar file. No external database. The file describes itself.

The Two-Zone Metadata Model

The cog specification uses a two-zone metadata model. In markdown, these appear as two sections of the YAML frontmatter. In other carriers, the same two zones are expressed through the carrier’s native metadata format.

Zone 1 carries document identity: title, version, description, author, created, modified. These fields are universal — they apply to any file regardless of context. In JavaScript, these are standard JSDoc tags (@description, @version, @author). In HTML, they are standard meta tags (<meta name="description">, <meta name="author">). Any tool that reads the native format gets the basics.

Zone 2 (under the mx: namespace) carries MX-operational metadata: status, contentType, tags, audience, relationships, licensing, AI policy fields. These fields are specific to the MX ecosystem and carry the governance, trust, and discovery information that machines need to act on files confidently. In JavaScript, these appear as @mx:status, @mx:contentType. In HTML, as <meta name="mx:status">. The namespace prefix makes MX fields distinguishable from standard metadata in every carrier format.

This separation is deliberate. Zone 1 works anywhere — any tool that reads the native format gets the basics. Zone 2 adds the MX layer for tools that understand the ecosystem. A cog degrades gracefully: a tool that knows nothing about MX still gets title, version, and description. A tool that understands MX gets everything.

The Economics of Metadata

The economic argument for cogs mirrors the argument for MX on websites, but the numbers are different.

When a machine reads a web page, it processes HTML — a few kilobytes to a few hundred kilobytes of structured content. The inference cost is measurable but bounded. When a machine reads an unstructured document — a 40-page PDF, a lengthy Word file, a sprawling wiki page — the token cost multiplies. The machine must read the entire document to extract basic facts that metadata would provide in a few hundred bytes.

Consider a large language model processing a document request. With cog metadata, the system reads the frontmatter (perhaps 200 tokens), determines whether this document is relevant, current, and authoritative, and either uses it or moves on. Without metadata, the system reads the entire document (perhaps 15,000 tokens), extracts the relevant information, and still cannot confirm whether the document is current or authoritative. The per-document cost difference is small. Across an organisation with thousands of documents, queried thousands of times per day, the aggregate difference is substantial.

Rich metadata does not just save compute — it improves accuracy. Every field in the frontmatter is a fact the machine does not have to infer from prose. Inference is probabilistic. Metadata is deterministic. A version: "3.0" field is unambiguous. A sentence buried in paragraph seven saying “this updates our previous policy” requires the machine to identify which previous policy, determine whether this document is the most recent update, and decide whether “updates” means “replaces” or “supplements.” The metadata eliminates the ambiguity. The machine reads a fact instead of constructing an interpretation.

Info-Cogs and Action-Cogs

The cog format supports two modes. Info-cogs describe, document, and explain. They are the data files of the MX ecosystem — structured content that any process can read.

Action-cogs are cogs that turn. They carry an execute block that declares what the cog does, what runtime it requires, and how to invoke it. An action-cog is simultaneously its own documentation and its own executable specification.

execute:
  runtime: runbook
  command: mx cog pricing validate
  actions:
    - name: validate
      description: Check pricing data for range errors
      inputs:
        - name: url
          type: string
          required: true
          description: The URL to validate
      outputs:
        - name: report
          type: markdown
          description: Validation findings

This is not a script. It is a declaration. The action-cog describes what it does, what it needs, and what it produces. The runtime executes it. The document IS the program specification. The runtime IS the interpreter.

This distinction — info-cog versus action-cog — is foundational to the MX ecosystem. Every action-cog is a cog. Not every cog is an action-cog. The presence of an execute block is the dividing line. Info-cogs sit still. Action-cogs turn.

Cogs and Skills

A pattern emerges as organisations adopt AI agents: alongside the content that agents read, teams create instructions that tell agents how to behave. These instructions go by various names — skills, prompts, system instructions, playbooks, runbooks — but they share a common shape: structured guidance that activates in a specific agent context and shapes the agent’s decisions.

This creates two categories of machine-readable document that are easily confused. Both are structured. Both carry metadata. Both guide automated systems. They serve fundamentally different architectural roles, and conflating them leads to fragile systems.

A cog is content. It describes itself — what it is, who wrote it, what it relates to, whether it is current, what audience it serves. The metadata is intrinsic to the document. Any machine, in any environment, at any time, can read the frontmatter and understand the document without reading the prose. A cog does not know which agent will read it, does not care which runtime processes it, and does not change its meaning based on context. The cog format is universal precisely because it makes no assumptions about the consumer.

A skill is an instruction. It tells a specific agent how to act in a specific context — what to check before modifying a database schema, what style conventions to follow when writing documentation, what sequence to use when deploying infrastructure. A skill activates when conditions are met: a keyword appears in a request, a file path matches a pattern, a content signature is detected. When activated, the skill injects contextual guidance into the agent’s decision-making process. Outside that agent runtime, the skill has no effect.

The relationship is complementary, not competitive:

  • A skill provides the trigger — “when the user mentions deployment, surface the deployment procedure and apply these guardrails.”
  • A cog provides the content — the deployment procedure itself, with structured metadata, version tracking, an executable action block if appropriate, and (for public documentation) cryptographic attestation via Reginald.

The skill ensures the agent finds the right cog at the right moment. The cog ensures the information is accurate, current, and machine-readable regardless of which agent reads it or how that agent was configured.

Dimension Cog Skill
Purpose Self-describing content Agent operational guidance
Consumer Any machine, any environment A specific agent in a specific runtime
Activation Pulled — an agent reads or queries for it Pushed — triggered by conditions in the agent’s context
Lifecycle Versioned, registered, discoverable across systems Scoped to agent sessions and configurations
Execution Action-cogs are self-executing (embedded procedures) Skills never execute — they shape agent behaviour
Dependencies Declares relationships (buildsOn, replaces, refersTo) References cogs but carries no dependency model
Portability Works across agents, runtimes, and organisations Tied to one agent platform’s conventions

The architectural implication is clear: cogs are infrastructure; skills are configuration.

An organisation that writes excellent cogs — rich metadata, clear descriptions, well-maintained versions — produces content that works for every agent that encounters it. The content is durable. When a new AI provider emerges, the cogs still work. When the organisation switches agent platforms, the cogs still work. When a partner organisation’s agent queries Reginald and discovers the documentation, the cogs still work. The investment in structured content compounds over time.

Skills, by contrast, are valuable but inherently coupled to a specific agent’s architecture. They optimise a workflow for a particular tool. When the tool changes — and tools change frequently — the skills must be rewritten. The investment in skills pays off immediately but does not transfer.

This is not an argument against skills. Organisations need both. The argument is about sequencing: invest in cogs first. Structured, self-describing content is the foundation. Skills are the optimisation layer that makes specific agents more effective at finding and acting on that content. Build the foundation before optimising the surface.

The parallel to web development is direct. A website with excellent semantic HTML, complete Schema.org markup, and clear metadata works for every search engine, every screen reader, every AI agent. A website that relies on platform-specific hacks to appear in one search engine’s results is fragile. The MX principle — design for both audiences — applies equally to documents: design content for every machine, then optimise the agent experience through skills where the workflow demands it.

Security and Runtime Constraints

An action-cog that can validate pricing data, install dependencies, or access contacts databases requires more than trust and access control. It requires runtime constraints — explicit declarations of what the cog is permitted to do when it executes.

Every action-cog carries a riskLevel classification in its frontmatter:

  • low — read-only, no side effects. Execute without confirmation.
  • medium — reads external data, produces reports. Warn before executing.
  • high — modifies filesystem, installs dependencies, handles credentials. Require explicit authorisation.
  • critical — destructive operations, confidential data, financial transactions. Require guardrail gate and full audit.

This classification is distinct from trust level. Trust measures provenance quality — is this cog genuine? Risk measures execution danger — how much damage can it cause if it runs? A cog can be fully attested and registered (high trust) and still dangerous to execute (high risk). Both signals are needed.

Action-cogs with riskLevel: high or critical declare a security block:

security:
  scope:
    filesystem: [mx-crm/contacts/**]
    network: none
    dataBoundary: user
    allowedOperations: [read, write, create]
  audit:
    logLevel: full
    retention: 1y
    includeInputs: true
    includeOutputs: false
  dataProtection:
    outputClassification: confidential
    prohibitedFields: [password, apiKey]
    piiHandling: mask
  rateLimit:
    maxCalls: 10
    window: 1h
  allowedRoles: [admin]

The scope constrains what the cog may touch — which filesystem paths, whether it may reach the network, whose data it may access, and what operations are permitted. The audit block declares logging requirements. The data protection block governs output sensitivity — sensitivity classification, prohibited fields, and redaction rules. The rate limit prevents abuse. The allowed roles bridge the guardrail pattern by declaring which roles the gate should verify.

These fields are declarations of intent. The cog states its boundaries so readers can enforce them. A reader that does not understand the security block ignores it — this is reader agency, the same principle that governs every other cog block. A reader that does understand it can enforce infrastructure-level authorisation before any action executes.

The security model draws on AgentLock, an open authorisation standard that addresses what it calls the “Full Permission anti-pattern”: AI agents executing tool calls with no infrastructure-level permission model. Traditional computing solved this decades ago with Unix file permissions, database GRANT/REVOKE, and cloud IAM. The security block brings the same discipline to cogs. The fact that such frameworks need to be built proves the point made throughout this book: the data project must precede the AI project. Governance declared at the tool level — before any agent runs — is the only governance that scales.

The practical implications are significant. An organisation’s standard operating procedures can be written as action-cogs. The procedure is simultaneously human-readable documentation (the markdown) and machine-executable specification (the execute block). When the procedure changes, the documentation changes with it — because they are the same file. The drift between “what the documentation says” and “what the system does” that plagues every large organisation is eliminated by architecture, not discipline.

The Core Action-Cogs

MX Reginald ships with core action-cogs that audit websites for machine readiness. Each one validates a specific aspect of the MX patterns described in this book:

  • Accessibility — Pa11y and axe-core validation against WCAG standards
  • Schema.org — structured data validation and completeness
  • Semantic HTML — heading hierarchy, landmark roles, DOM structure
  • Metadata — Open Graph, Twitter Cards, meta tag completeness
  • Pricing — range-error detection (the £203,000 problem from Chapter 2)
  • Readability — plain language analysis for human and machine audiences
  • Link validation — broken link detection across the site
  • Sitemap analysis — completeness and structure validation
  • robots.txt — AI crawler stance analysis
  • llms.txt — generation and validation of machine discovery files
  • Toast detection — ephemeral UI that machines cannot see
  • Clarity — documentation clarity and completeness analysis
  • Cog validation — specification conformance checking

Each action-cog is self-describing. A machine that encounters one knows what it does, how to run it, what inputs it needs, and what outputs it produces — all from the frontmatter. No external documentation required.

Reginald — The Registry

Cogs are self-describing by design. A .cog.md file in a repository, on a server, or in a CMS is already machine-readable. It works for the teams and tools that have access to it. No registration. No external dependency. No infrastructure beyond a file system.

Self-description solves only half the problem. The other half is discovery and trust.

The Discovery Problem

An AI agent is asked about a product’s maintenance schedule. The manufacturer has published excellent documentation — a cog with rich metadata, clear procedures, and current information. The agent does not know this documentation exists. It has never crawled the manufacturer’s site. It was not trained on the document. It has no way to discover that structured, authoritative documentation is available.

The agent does what it always does: it searches the web, finds fragments of information on forums, review sites, and third-party blogs, and constructs a plausible but unreliable answer. The authoritative documentation exists. The agent cannot find it.

This is the discovery problem. Self-describing documents are valuable. Discoverable, self-describing documents are transformative.

The Trust Problem

Discovery alone is insufficient. Once a machine finds a document, it must determine whether to trust it. Is this the genuine document published by the claimed author? Has it been modified since publication? Is it the current version, or has it been superseded?

On the open web, these questions are difficult to answer. Anyone can publish a document claiming to be the official maintenance guide for a product. Without cryptographic verification, a machine cannot distinguish the genuine article from a modified copy, an outdated version, or a deliberate forgery.

What Reginald Provides

Reginald addresses both problems. It is a public registry where cogs can be registered, discovered, and verified. The registry comprises three capabilities:

Discovery. Registered cogs are indexed and queryable. AI providers can query the registry at inference time: “Is there registered documentation for this product?” The registry returns metadata, location, and trust information. The machine can then fetch the document directly from the publisher — Reginald indexes metadata, not content.

Attestation. The signing engine applies Ed25519 cryptographic signatures to cogs. A signed cog carries a Certificate of Genuineness (COG) — proof that a specific publisher created this specific document at this specific time, and that the content has not been modified since signing. The signature is verifiable by anyone with the public key. No centralised authority required.

Currency. The registry tracks versions. When a publisher updates a document and registers the new version, machines querying the registry receive the current metadata. Superseded versions are marked as such. The “three-versions-old PDF” problem described at the start of this chapter is solved by architecture.

The Compliance Levels

The registry defines compliance levels that reflect increasing degrees of structure and trust:

Level 1 — Basic. Valid YAML frontmatter. Publisher identified. The document is a cog, but minimally structured. Sufficient for internal use where trust is implicit.

Level 2 — Structured. MX-compliant format with description, status, contentType, and tags. The document follows the specification and can be processed by any MX-aware tool.

Level 3 — Verified. Cryptographically signed. The Ed25519 signature establishes provenance and integrity. This is the minimum level for Reginald registration. Below this threshold, the document is a cog but not a registered, attested cog.

Level 4 — Certified. All MX fields present. Full metadata coverage. The document is a complete, specification-conformant cog with cryptographic attestation.

Level 5 — Audited. Third-party verified. An independent audit confirms that the document meets all specification requirements and that the metadata accurately reflects the content. This level is planned but not yet operational.

These levels are not gatekeeping. They are a progression. Most cogs will be Level 1 or Level 2 — internal documents with structured metadata, used by the teams and tools that create them. Only cogs that cross organisational boundaries — public documentation, API references, compliance records — benefit from the higher levels.

The Registry API

Reginald exposes a REST API for machine consumption:

  • Cog listing — all registered cogs, filterable by namespace, tags, and status
  • Cog metadata — full metadata and certificate for a specific cog
  • Raw content — the document itself, served from the publisher’s infrastructure
  • Statistics — registry health, cog counts, and activity metrics
  • Public key — the Ed25519 public key for signature verification
  • Machine discovery — an llms.txt file that describes the registry for AI agents

The API is designed for machines. No authentication required for read access. Content is served with appropriate caching headers. The registry is the index, not the warehouse — documents live with their publishers, and the registry points machines to the authoritative source.

Where Cogs Live

Cogs have no residency requirement. They work wherever files work, and most will never leave the environment where they were created.

On a developer’s laptop. A personal cog sitting in ~/notes/ or ~/projects/. Only the developer and their local AI assistant can read it. The metadata is already useful — the AI agent knows what the file is about without reading the content. No network, no server, no registration.

On a company file server. The same cog, moved to a shared drive or a NAS. Every team member and every AI tool with access to that drive can now read the metadata. The cog did not change. Its audience grew. No infrastructure changes needed — the metadata was already there.

In a git repository. The cog is versioned, branched, reviewed. Pull requests review metadata alongside content. The git history provides an audit trail. For most development teams, this is the natural home — cogs travel with the code they describe.

In a CMS or SharePoint. The file sits where it always sat. The metadata makes it self-describing for any machine that encounters it. A document management system that supports YAML frontmatter or the file’s native metadata format can index and surface cogs without any new tooling.

On a public website. An HTML page with <meta name="mx:*"> tags, a markdown file served from a documentation site, a JSON-LD manifest — all cogs, all machine-readable, all discoverable by any crawler that visits. Discovery still depends on the machine finding the page in the first place.

Published in Reginald. The cog is now registered in a public index. Any AI agent, anywhere, can query the registry and find it. The signing engine has attested it — cryptographic proof of authorship and integrity. Version tracking ensures machines always find the current edition. This is the only level that requires external infrastructure.

The progression is not mandatory. Most cogs will live in git repositories and company file servers for their entire useful life. They do their job — eliminating guessing for every machine that reads them — without ever touching a registry. Reginald exists for the minority of cogs that need to cross organisational boundaries with trust and discoverability.

When You Need Reginald (and When You Do Not)

This distinction is critical, and getting it wrong in either direction wastes effort.

You do not need Reginald when:

  • Your cogs are local or private — on a laptop, a file server, a shared drive
  • Your cogs live in a git repository used by your own team
  • Trust is implicit because the files live within your organisation’s boundaries
  • Discovery is not a problem because your tools know where to find the files
  • You are starting with the cog format and building internal capability

In these cases, the cog format is the value. Structured metadata in the file’s native carrier format. Machine-readable and human-readable in the same file. No registration, no signing, no external dependency. A .cog.md file works anywhere a markdown file works. An HTML file with <meta name="mx:*"> tags works anywhere an HTML file works. A shell script with MX metadata in its comments works anywhere the script works.

You need Reginald when:

  • Attestation — you need to prove a file is genuine and unmodified. Regulatory compliance, legal documentation, safety-critical procedures, API contracts. The signing engine provides Ed25519 cryptographic validation that any tool can verify.
  • Maintenance — you publish living documentation and need machines to find the current version reliably. Product manuals, API references, pricing schedules, compliance policies. The registry tracks what is current and what has been superseded.
  • Public discovery — you want AI agents beyond your own organisation to find, trust, and use your documentation. The registry makes your cogs discoverable at inference time.

The analogy is precise: a website works without Google indexing it. A cog works without Reginald registering it. A cog on a company file server is already doing its job. Registration adds discovery and trust for cogs that cross organisational boundaries. Below that threshold, the format stands entirely on its own.

The Network Effect

Reginald’s value grows with adoption. A registry with ten cogs is a curiosity. A registry with ten thousand cogs — covering major product lines, API references, compliance frameworks, and industry standards — becomes infrastructure that AI providers query by default.

This network effect is the strategic rationale. The cog format is open (MIT licensed, governed by The Gathering). The registry is the product. As more publishers register authoritative documentation, AI agents that query the registry produce more accurate answers. More accurate answers drive more queries. More queries drive more registrations.

The model parallels DNS. The Domain Name System is a registry that maps names to addresses. Anyone can run a web server without registering a domain name — but nobody does, because discoverability requires it. Reginald maps documents to trust. Anyone can publish a cog without registering it — and many should, for internal use. When documents need to be discovered and trusted by machines outside your organisation, the registry is where that trust is established.

A closer parallel is npm — the package registry that transformed how developers share code. Every npm package carries a package.json: structured metadata declaring what the package does, who wrote it, what version it is, what it depends on, and what licence governs it. Before npm, developers copied library files between projects, guessed at versions, and hoped for compatibility. The registry changed that. A developer runs npm install and gets the right version of the right package with its dependencies resolved. The metadata does the work.

Reginald does the same thing for machines reading content. A published cog carries structured metadata declaring what the document is, who published it, what version is current, and what it relates to. Before a registry, an AI agent crawls the web, finds fragments, and guesses at provenance and currency. With the registry, the agent queries Reginald and gets the authoritative version of the authoritative document with its trust chain verified. The metadata does the work.

The structural parallels are precise:

npm Reginald
package.json Cog frontmatter
Package name and version Title, version, replaces
dependencies buildsOn, refersTo
npm publish Cog registration + signing
npm registry Reginald registry
npm install (resolved, verified) Agent query (resolved, attested)
Scoped packages (@org/pkg) Namespaced cogs
README.md Markdown body (human-readable)

The difference is the consumer. npm serves developers building software. Reginald serves machines consuming content. The principle is identical: self-describing packages in a public registry, discoverable and verifiable by anyone, eliminate the guessing that unstructured distribution creates.

This framing matters commercially. Every developer understands what npm did for code reuse. Reginald does the same thing for documentation, product information, policy documents, API references — any content that machines need to find, trust, and act on accurately. Published cogs are npm for machines.

The Broader Picture

Cogs and Reginald complete the MX architecture. The Handbook’s patterns make websites machine-readable at the page level. The cog format makes documents machine-readable at the file level. Reginald makes both discoverable and trustworthy at the network level.

The progression is:

  1. Fix your websites — semantic HTML, Schema.org, explicit state, heading hierarchy (this book, The Handbook)
  2. Fix your documents — structured metadata, machine-readable frontmatter, the cog format (the format is free, open, and immediate)
  3. Publish with trust — cryptographic attestation, version tracking, public discovery (Reginald, when you need it)

Each level builds on the one below. You cannot meaningfully attest documents that lack structured metadata. You cannot meaningfully register documents that are not self-describing. The dependency chain runs in one direction, just like the Three-Layer IA Framework from Chapter 18: fix the foundation first, then build upward.

The cog format costs nothing to adopt. It requires no tooling, no registration, and no infrastructure beyond a text editor. For a markdown file, the barrier to entry is three fields and two --- lines. For an HTML page, it is a single <meta> tag. For a JavaScript file, a JSDoc comment. For a shell script, a commented YAML block. Every file you already have can become self-describing for machines. Start there. When your files need to cross organisational boundaries with provenance and discoverability, Reginald is ready.

Glossary of Terms

A

Accessibility The practice of making websites usable by people with disabilities. The book argues that patterns that work for machines often also improve accessibility for screen readers, keyboard navigation, and assistive technologies.

Agent (or AI Agent) One type of machine that reads the web. An artificial intelligence system that acts on behalf of a human user to complete tasks. Examples include ChatGPT browsing the web, Claude with computer use capabilities, or browser extensions with AI functionality. MX uses “machine” as the umbrella term for all software that reads websites — AI agents are one category alongside crawlers, voice assistants, browser automation tools, and local models.

Machine Types (Five Primary Categories) This book uses five standardised machine types aligned with MX: The Handbook:

  1. Server-Side Agents (ChatGPT, Claude) — Run on remote servers, fetch raw HTML text only, cannot execute JavaScript or render CSS.

  2. In-Browser Agents (Microsoft Copilot, browser extensions) — Run within web browsers with full DOM access, can execute JavaScript, inherit authenticated sessions and cookies.

  3. Browser Automation Agents (Perplexity, Playwright-based) — Control browsers programmatically, can take screenshots and use computer vision, see layout and colour relationships.

  4. Local Agents (Ollama, Claude Code, Cline) — Run on users’ personal computers with limited resources and context windows, includes CLI tools and privacy-focused implementations.

  5. Agentic Operating Systems (Anthropic Cowork) — Orchestrate multiple machines in parallel, combine capabilities of other types for complex multi-step workflows.

Each type has different capabilities for JavaScript execution, session access, state detection, and authentication. See Chapter 1 for detailed explanations.

Machine-Friendly Design Web design patterns that work well for both human users and machines. Characterised by explicit state, persistent errors, complete information, and semantic structure.

Machine-Hostile Pattern A design pattern that works for humans but breaks for machines. Examples include toast notifications, forced pagination, and validation that occurs only after form submission.

Agentic Commerce Protocol (ACP) An open-source protocol (Apache 2.0 license) for machine-mediated commerce, announced by OpenAI and Stripe in September 2024. ACP enables machines to complete purchases on behalf of users whilst preserving merchant-of-record relationships and avoiding platform lock-in. Over 1 million merchants on Shopify and Etsy support ACP. Powers “Instant Checkout” in ChatGPT. See Chapter 9 for competitive analysis with Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP) and Microsoft Copilot Checkout.

ai-* meta tags Proposed naming convention for HTML meta tags that provide guidance to machines. Not yet standardised, but follows the pattern of existing meta tag conventions like robots and viewport. Examples include ai-api-endpoint, mx:content-policy, and mx:attribution. These proposed patterns use the mx: namespace to avoid conflicts with existing standards and remain harmless if machines don’t recognise them.

ai-agent-instructions Meta tag dynamically injected by JavaScript handshake scripts to provide session-specific guidance to browser-based machines. Typically contains instructions about prioritising certain resources (like llms.txt) and citation requirements. Not typically present in static HTML — instead injected when AI User-Agents are detected.

API (Application Programming Interface) A structured way for programs to interact with a service. APIs provide machine-readable data that machines can consume more reliably than scraping HTML.

Attribution Crediting the source of information. When a machine summarises content from a website, proper attribution includes citing the source with a link back to the original.

B

Bot Detection Technologies designed to identify and block automated access to websites. Often creates an arms race between sites that try to block machines and machines that try to appear human.

Browser Extension Software that adds functionality to web browsers. AI-powered browser extensions can read and interact with web pages, potentially inheriting the user’s authenticated sessions.

C

CAPTCHA (Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart) A challenge-response test designed to determine whether a user is human. Common examples include selecting images with traffic lights or solving puzzles. Blocks many machines from accessing sites.

Citation In the context of Generative Engine Optimisation (GEO), a citation occurs when a machine references your website as a source in its response to a user query. Unlike traditional SEO where success is measured by clicks and page views, GEO success is measured by how often machines cite your content. Citations typically include attribution with a link back to the source. See Chapter 10 for the fundamental distinction between citation-based and click-based metrics.

Client-Side Code that runs in the user’s web browser rather than on the server. Client-side validation happens in the browser before data is sent to the server.

Cookie Consent Banner The pop-up that appears on European websites asks users to accept or reject cookies. Required by GDPR, but creates barriers for machines that don’t understand how to interact with them.

Computational Trust The compounding credibility a machine builds toward a website through repeated successful interactions. Each time a machine extracts accurate data, completes a transaction, or receives well-structured responses, that site’s reliability score increases. Over time, machines preferentially route to high-trust sites — recommending them more confidently and returning more frequently. Computational trust is a first-mover advantage: sites that earn it early become increasingly difficult to displace.

Convergence Principle The observation that design patterns that work well for machines also tend to work well for humans with disabilities, users of assistive technology, or anyone in non-ideal conditions.

D

data-agent-visible HTML attribute pattern for marking metadata that should be visible to machines but hidden from human users. Uses CSS display: none; to hide from visual rendering whilst remaining in the DOM for machine parsing. This experimental pattern follows the convention of data-* attributes for custom metadata and provides a semantic marker that machines can search for when looking for hidden instructions or structured information.

Delegation The process of granting a machine permission to act on your behalf with specific, limited permissions. Secure delegation uses tokens rather than sharing passwords.

Delegation Token A credential that grants a machine specific, time-limited permissions to act on a user’s behalf. Unlike passwords, tokens can be scoped to particular actions and automatically expire.

DOM (Document Object Model) The tree structure represents a web page’s content. Machines parse the DOM to understand page structure and extract information.

Entity Asset Layer (EAL) A strategic framework for organising an entity’s digital assets into four categories: Identity (who you are), Reputation (what others say about you), Knowledge (what you know and publish), and Transactional (what you can do). The EAL makes these assets sovereign and portable — owned by the entity rather than locked into any single platform. When assets are structured with MX patterns, platforms become interchangeable view layers rather than sources of truth.

E

Ephemeral Error An error message that appears temporarily and then disappears. Toast notifications are ephemeral errors. They’re problematic because machines may miss them entirely.

Extraction The process of a machine reading and summarising content from a website. Raises questions about copyright, fair use, and compensation for content creators.

MX Readiness Model (0-5) The framework describing how AI agents interact with websites, progressing through six sequential levels: Level 0 — Not Ready (no deliberate MX intent), Level 1 — Basic (agents can discover), Level 2 — Structured (agents can cite and attribute), Level 3 — Attested (agents can compare and recommend), Level 4 — Registered (agents can transact with confidence), and Level 5 — Audited (agents can guarantee accuracy). Each level builds on the one below — skip a level and everything above it is unreachable.

F

False Positive When an agent reports success despite actually failing to complete a task. Occurs when the agent misses error messages and assumes everything worked correctly. More dangerous than apparent failures.

FIDO2/WebAuthn Authentication standards used by hardware security keys like YubiKeys. Prove physical presence through cryptographic signatures. Difficult for remote AI agents to use.

Form Validation The process of validating whether form inputs meet requirements (correct format, required fields, etc.). Synchronous validation checks inputs immediately; asynchronous validation checks only after submission.

G

GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation) European privacy law regulates how personal data is collected and processed. Affects how AI agents can access and use personal information.

GEO (Generative Engine Optimisation) The practice of optimising websites to be cited by AI agents in their responses to user queries. Unlike traditional SEO (Search Engine Optimisation) which optimises for clicks and page views, GEO optimises for citations and attribution. Key techniques include structured data (Schema.org), semantic HTML, llms.txt files, and clear content organisation. See Chapter 10 for detailed guidance on implementing GEO strategies.

Global Privacy Control (GPC) A browser signal indicating the user wants minimal tracking. If agents set this header and sites respect it, cookie consent banners become unnecessary.

GTIN (Global Trade Item Number) International product identifier used in barcodes and structured data. Includes formats like UPC (12 digits, primarily North America), EAN-13 (13 digits, global), and ISBN (books). Including GTIN in Schema.org Product markup helps AI agents uniquely identify products across different retailers and prevent confusion between similar items.

H

HATEOAS (Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State) A REST architectural principle that suggests APIs should include links describing available actions. Theoretically helpful for agents, but it never gained widespread adoption.

Headless Browser A web browser without a graphical interface, often used for automation and testing. Many AI agents use headless browsers to interact with websites.

I

Identity Layer (see Missing Identity Layer)

Identity Token A cryptographic token that proves a customer’s identity when an agent acts on their behalf. Various approaches are being developed for how these tokens are issued, verified, and scoped and used to preserve customer relationships (loyalty, warranty) in agent-mediated transactions.

Information Architecture (IA) The practice of organising, structuring, and labelling content to support findability and usability. Traditional IA optimises for human wayfinding — clear navigation, consistent labelling, logical hierarchy. Machine-focused IA optimises for the same goals but for different visitors: AI agents that parse DOM trees, follow sitemaps, and extract structured data. The Three-Layer IA Framework organises machine-readable structure at three scales: the site layer (sitemaps, URL hierarchy, internal linking), the page layer (heading hierarchy, landmark roles, DOM ordering), and the content layer (semantic HTML, Schema.org, inline semantics). See Chapter 17 for the unified framework.

Invisible Users The book’s term for AI agents. Called “invisible” because they’re invisible to most site owners (blend into analytics) and the interface is partly invisible to them (can’t see animations or subtle visual cues).

J

JSON-LD (JavaScript Object Notation for Linked Data) A format for adding structured, machine-readable data to web pages. Uses Schema.org vocabularies to describe products, businesses, events, and other content in ways both search engines and AI agents can parse reliably.

L

llms.txt An emerging convention for providing site-wide guidance to AI agents. Similar to robots.txt but designed specifically for large language models.

Loading State The visual cue that content is loading. Spinners, progress bars, and skeleton screens are loading states. Problematic for agents because there’s no standard way to determine when loading is complete.

Loyalty Programme A customer rewards system where repeat purchases earn points or benefits. Breaks when AI agents make purchases because the retailer doesn’t know who the actual customer is.

M

Machine Experience (MX) The practice of adding metadata and instructions to internet assets so AI agents do not have to think. When AI must infer meaning from incomplete or ambiguous context, it hallucinates. Explicit structure prevents this. MX builds on established web standards — semantic HTML, WCAG accessibility, Schema.org structured data, Open Graph, Dublin Core — and adds governance metadata where those standards leave gaps. A well-built MX page is simultaneously a well-built SEO page, an accessible page, and a GEO page.

MCP (Model Context Protocol) An open protocol developed by Anthropic that provides a standardised way for AI models to interact with external tools and data sources. MCP enables agents to call functions, read files, and access APIs through a structured interface. See also WebMCP, which extends this concept to web browsers.

Microdata A specification for embedding machine-readable data in HTML. Similar to JSON-LD but integrated directly into HTML tags using itemscope and itemprop attributes.

Morning-After Test A simple, immediately actionable test for machine readability. Paste a page’s HTML into a large language model and ask it to extract specific information (price, availability, contact details, next steps). If the model struggles, agents will struggle too. The test works because it simulates the worst-case agent scenario — raw HTML parsing without JavaScript execution, visual rendering, or session context.

Missing Identity Layer The problem identified in Chapter 4 is that when AI agents make purchases on behalf of customers, businesses lose direct contact with the customer. Prevents loyalty programmes, warranty registration, and customer relationship management from functioning. Various solutions are being developed, including retailer-specific tokens, centralised repositories, blockchain attestations, and browser-native delegation.

MPN (Manufacturer Part Number) A unique identifier assigned by the manufacturer to distinguish a specific product. Including MPN in Schema.org Product markup helps AI agents identify the exact product model across different retailers, preventing confusion between similar items from the same manufacturer. Particularly useful for electronics, appliances, and industrial products.

O

OAuth2 (Open Authorisation 2.0) The industry-standard protocol (RFC 6749) for secure authorisation. Often proposed as one approach for agent identity delegation.

P

Pagination Splitting content across multiple pages. Common for product listings, search results, and long-form content. Problematic for agents because they may not discover that additional pages exist.

Persistent Error An error message that remains visible until the user resolves it. Better for both humans and agents than ephemeral errors that disappear after a few seconds.

Progressive Enhancement A web design strategy that builds pages in layers: a solid HTML foundation that works without CSS or JavaScript, enhanced with CSS for visual presentation, then enhanced further with JavaScript for interactive behaviour. Each layer works without the next. For AI agents, this guarantees that the content and structure are accessible even when the agent cannot execute JavaScript — which is the case for server-side agents that fetch raw HTML.

Progressive Disclosure A UX pattern that hides information until the user requests it. Reduces cognitive load for humans but hides information from agents. Examples include tabs, accordions, and “show more” buttons.

R

Rate Limiting Restricting the number of requests a user or agent can make within a given time period. Prevents abuse but can block legitimate agent use if limits are too strict.

robots.txt A file that tells web crawlers which parts of a site they can access. Respected by search engines but inconsistently honoured by AI agents.

S

Schema.org A collaborative project creating vocabularies for structured data on web pages. Provides standardised ways to describe products, businesses, events, recipes, and hundreds of other content types.

Screen Reader Assistive technology that reads web content aloud for visually impaired users. Requires semantic HTML and proper structure — the same things AI agents need.

SEO (Search Engine Optimisation) The practice of optimising websites to rank higher in search engine results pages (SERPs). Traditional SEO measures success by clicks and page views. Increasingly converging with GEO (Generative Engine Optimisation) as search engines integrate AI-generated answers that cite sources rather than just listing links. See Chapter 10 for analysis of GEO vs SEO convergence.

SKU (Stock Keeping Unit) An internal product code assigned by retailers to track inventory. Unlike GTIN or MPN which are standardised across retailers, each retailer creates its own SKUs. Including SKU in Schema.org Product markup helps with inventory management but provides less value for cross-retailer product identification.

Semantic HTML HTML that conveys the meaning of content, not just its appearance. Uses elements like <article>, <nav>, <main> instead of generic <div> tags. Essential for both accessibility and agent comprehension.

Server-Side Code that runs on the web server rather than in the user’s browser. Server-side validation happens on the server after data is submitted.

Session A period of interaction between a user and a website, typically maintained through cookies. Sessions store authentication state and user preferences.

Session Inheritance The security problem where browser-based AI agents inherit a user’s authenticated session, including all proof-of-humanity tokens and authentication credentials. Makes it impossible for banks and other services to detect AI involvement.

Single-Page Application (SPA) A web application that updates content dynamically without full page reloads. Provides smooth user experience but creates ambiguity about state changes that confuses AI agents.

State The current condition of a web page or application. Examples include “loading,” “complete,” “error,” or “form valid.” Explicit state attributes make it clear to agents what’s happening.

Structured Data Machine-readable information about page content. Includes JSON-LD, microdata, and other formats that describe what content means rather than just how it looks.

Synchronous Validation Form validation that happens immediately as the user types or completes fields, rather than waiting until form submission. Better for both humans and agents.

T

Toast Notification A brief message that appears temporarily (often 2-5 seconds) and then disappears. Named after toast popping out of a toaster. A significant source of agent failures is agents’ failure to detect ephemeral messages.

TOTP (Time-Based One-Time Password) A 6-digit code that changes every 30 seconds, generated by authenticator apps like Google Authenticator. Uses a shared cryptographic seed to create codes. Blocks AI agents unless they have access to the seed.

Two-Factor Authentication (2FA) Security requires two factors of proof of identity (typically a password and an SMS code, an authenticator app, or a hardware token). Increases security but blocks most AI agent access.

U

Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP) An open protocol for agent-mediated commerce announced by Google in January 2026 at the National Retail Federation conference. UCP enables AI agents to complete purchases through Google’s Business Agent (which surfaces in search results) whilst maintaining merchant-of-record relationships. Backed by 20+ major retailers including Target, Walmart, Macy’s, Best Buy, and The Home Depot. Claims compatibility with Agentic Commerce Protocol (ACP) and existing infrastructure protocols (A2A, AP2, MCP), though technical interoperability remains unverified. See Chapter 9 for analysis of fragmentation risk between UCP and ACP, and Microsoft Copilot Checkout’s competitive isolation.

User-Agent An HTTP header identifying the browser or application making a request. Many agent detection systems check this header, but it’s easily spoofed.

W

Worst-Agent Principle The design rule that sites should be built to work for the most constrained AI agent, not the most capable. A significant proportion of deployed models have fewer than 100 million parameters and run on phones, kiosk displays, and warehouse scanners with severely limited context windows. If a constrained local model can parse a page, every agent can. This mirrors the accessibility principle of designing for the most limited user — and produces the same beneficial results for everyone.

Warranty Registration Recording who owns a product to honour warranty claims. Breaks when AI agents make purchases because the retailer doesn’t know the customer’s identity.

Web Scraping Extracting data from websites by parsing HTML. Less reliable than using APIs because the HTML structure can change without warning.

WebMCP (Web Model Context Protocol) A W3C draft standard (February 2026) developed by Google and Microsoft that lets websites expose structured, callable tools to AI agents through a browser API. WebMCP provides the action layer – agents can invoke registered functions like searchProducts() or bookTable() instead of scraping DOM elements. Complements MX, which provides the understanding layer through structured metadata. Together they form the two halves of the companion web. See Appendix J for industry context and Appendix L for implementation patterns.

Y

YubiKey A brand of hardware security token (FIDO2/WebAuthn device) that proves physical presence through cryptographic signatures. Provides strong security but blocks remote AI agents.

Note: This glossary covers technical terms used throughout the book. For more details on any concept, refer to the chapter where it’s introduced or the index.

The Machine Experience Manifesto

A vision for designing interfaces that serve both human and machine intelligence

Our Belief

We believe that the rise of AI agents as primary users of digital interfaces represents not a disruption, but an opportunity — an opportunity to build better experiences for everyone.

The same patterns that enable AI agents to navigate, understand, and act upon digital content also empower human users with disabilities, enhance accessibility, and create more robust, maintainable systems.

This is the Convergence Principle: interfaces optimised for machines inherently improve experiences for humans.

What is Machine Experience?

Machine Experience (MX) is the practice of designing and building digital interfaces with explicit recognition that AI agents are legitimate users deserving thoughtful design consideration.

Where User Experience (UX) focused exclusively on human interaction, Machine Experience acknowledges a fundamental shift: autonomous systems now browse websites, complete purchases, extract information, and make decisions without human intervention.

MX practitioners design for this reality whilst ensuring human users benefit equally from the improvements.

Core Principles

1. Semantic Clarity

Structure precedes presentation. Semantic HTML, explicit state management, and machine-readable metadata create interfaces that both humans and agents can reliably interpret.

2. Universal Accessibility

Patterns that work for AI agents also work for screen readers, keyboard navigation, and assistive technologies. MX is accessibility 2.0 — designing for the broadest possible range of users, human and machine alike.

3. Explicit State

Make system state visible and queryable. Agents and humans both benefit from knowing where they are, what actions are available, and what the consequences of those actions will be.

4. Progressive Disclosure

Information should be structured for both scanning and deep reading. Provide clear navigation, tables of contents, heading hierarchies, and semantic markup that allow both quick assessment and thorough investigation.

5. Standards Over Proprietary Solutions

Use established standards (Schema.org, semantic HTML, WCAG, ARIA) over custom implementations. Standards ensure broad compatibility across diverse user agents — human browsers, AI systems, and assistive technologies.

The MX metadata standard — structured documents — is developed through The Gathering, a community-led collection of repositories working to develop open standards that enable content to be understood, interpreted, and processed more consistently by both people and AI systems. Structured documents are markdown files with YAML frontmatter: machine-readable metadata at the top, human-readable documentation below. The Gathering develops the standards openly; implementers build products on them.

6. Transparency

Make your interfaces discoverable. Use llms.txt files, clear robots.txt policies, and structured metadata to communicate what your system offers and how agents should interact with it.

7. Ethical Design

Design for consent, not exploitation. AI agents should respect user preferences, honour opt-outs, and operate within clearly defined boundaries established by interface owners.

Who Uses MX Practice?

Machine Experience serves diverse practitioners — both human and machine:

AI Agents and Autonomous Systems

  • AI assistants parsing websites for information extraction
  • Browser-based agents navigating e-commerce platforms
  • CLI agents researching products and services
  • Search engines indexing structured content
  • Voice assistants querying web services
  • Autonomous purchasing agents completing transactions
  • Content aggregation systems processing metadata

AI agents are not just beneficiaries of MX — they are active practitioners. When an agent validates extracted data against Schema.org structured data, it practises MX. When it cross-references HTML content with JSON-LD, it practises MX. When it reports confidence scores and acknowledges uncertainty, it practises MX.

Human Practitioners

Developers and Engineers

  • Frontend developers implementing semantic HTML and ARIA patterns
  • Backend engineers designing APIs that serve both human UIs and autonomous agents
  • Full-stack developers building e-commerce, content platforms, and SaaS applications
  • DevOps engineers ensuring infrastructure supports both traditional and agent-based access patterns

UX and Design Professionals

  • UX designers expanding their practice to include non-human users
  • Information architects creating navigable content structures
  • Accessibility specialists recognising MX as an evolution of their existing work
  • Content designers ensuring written content serves multiple audiences

Business Leaders

  • Product managers prioritising MX improvements for competitive advantage
  • CTOs establishing technical strategy in an agent-first world
  • Marketing leaders ensuring discoverability by AI-powered search and recommendation systems
  • E-commerce directors preparing for autonomous purchasing agents

Content Creators and Publishers

  • Technical writers structuring documentation for both human reading and agent parsing
  • Bloggers and journalists making content discoverable and quotable by AI systems
  • Publishers adapting content delivery for agent consumption
  • Educators creating learning materials accessible to AI tutoring systems

Researchers and Academics

  • AI researchers studying agent-environment interactions
  • HCI specialists investigating machine-human interface design
  • Accessibility researchers exploring convergence between assistive technologies and AI agents
  • Information scientists developing standards and best practices

Advocacy and Community Organisers

  • Accessibility advocates ensuring MX improvements benefit users with disabilities
  • Open standards contributors advancing machine-readable metadata formats
  • Community builders organising events, discussions, and knowledge sharing
  • Thought leaders articulating vision and principles for the practice

Our Commitment

We commit to:

  1. Open Knowledge Sharing — Document patterns, share learnings, publish research, and contribute to community understanding
  2. Inclusive Community — Welcome practitioners from all backgrounds and experience levels
  3. Practical Implementation — Prioritise actionable guidance over theoretical discussion
  4. Standards Advancement — Contribute to open standards through The Gathering and resist proprietary lock-in
  5. Accessibility First — Never compromise human accessibility in pursuit of machine optimisation
  6. Transparent Development — Work in the open, accept feedback, and iterate based on real-world evidence
  7. Cross-Disciplinary Collaboration — Bridge gaps between developers, designers, accessibility advocates, and business stakeholders

What MX Is Not

Not all websites can or should optimise for AI agents.

MX is not a universal mandate. Some interfaces legitimately exclude automated access:

  • Banking and financial systems that require human verification for security
  • Healthcare portals protecting sensitive medical information
  • Authentication systems designed to prevent automated attacks
  • Rate-limited APIs protecting infrastructure from overload
  • Human-verification systems like CAPTCHAs serving legitimate security purposes

Not every optimisation is appropriate. Some websites prioritise visual design, artistic expression, or experimental interaction patterns that don’t translate to machine-readable structure. That’s valid. MX provides patterns for those who choose to implement them, not a requirement for all web content.

The choice to exclude agents should be intentional, not accidental. If you choose not to optimise for AI agents, make that explicit through robots.txt policies and clear documentation. Silent failures serve no one. Intentional exclusion with clear communication respects both human and machine users.

Why Open Source

This community operates under the MIT Licence — and that choice matters.

Why Not Proprietary Standards?

Proprietary standards create:

  • Vendor lock-in — Users trapped by incompatible implementations
  • Competitive moats — Companies profiting from artificial barriers
  • Fragmentation — Multiple incompatible “standards” competing
  • Reduced innovation — Closed systems limit contribution and improvement

Open standards enable:

  • Universal compatibility — One implementation works everywhere
  • Collective improvement — Community contributions strengthen patterns
  • Competitive choice — Users select tools based on merit, not lock-in
  • Ecosystem health — Rising tide lifts all boats

Connection to Convergence Principle

Open standards ARE convergence in practice. When Schema.org publishes vocabulary specifications openly, both humans (developers) and machines (agents) benefit from the same documentation. When WCAG guidelines are freely available, implementations improve accessibility for everyone.

Openness prevents the January 2026 problem: Three platforms launched agent commerce within seven days (Amazon, Microsoft, Google). Microsoft chose proprietary (Copilot Checkout). OpenAI/Stripe and Google chose open protocols (ACP and UCP). The proprietary system is now competitively isolated whilst the open protocols compete for convergence.

We choose open because closed standards contradict MX principles. If convergence means patterns that benefit both humans and machines, those patterns must be freely available to all practitioners. Proprietary MX would be a contradiction.

How MX Practice Evolves

AI technology changes. MX practices must adapt.

Technology Evolution

What works today may not work tomorrow:

  • LLM capabilities improve — Agents handle ambiguity better, but validation remains critical
  • Browser APIs evolve — New standards enable better agent-website communication
  • Platform consolidation — Competing standards (ACP vs UCP) eventually converge or one dominates
  • Security threats emerge — Agent-based attacks require new defensive patterns

MX patterns must evolve alongside these changes.

Learning Mechanisms

LEARNINGS.md documents mistakes. When AI agents fail (£203,000 pricing error), we document what went wrong and how to prevent it. These learnings become knowledge, save this along with your documents.

Discussion archives preserve insights. Industry developments, tool feedback, implementation patterns, and case studies capture collective wisdom. Future practitioners learn from documented experience.

Pattern refinement through practice. What seems like good theory gets tested in production. Patterns that work get refined. Patterns that fail get replaced. The community learns systematically.

Version Control for Principles

This manifesto is version-controlled. You can see its evolution through git history. When principles change, the history preserves context about why.

Principles evolve through community debate. We invite feedback, refinement, and challenge. When someone proves a principle wrong or incomplete, we update it. When new insights emerge, we incorporate them.

No principle is sacred. If convergence proves false in practice, we abandon it. If transparency creates more problems than it solves, we reconsider. Evidence and real-world implementation trump theoretical purity.

The community decides. Changes require discussion, consensus, and demonstration that new approaches serve practitioners better than old ones. Evolution happens through collective wisdom, not individual decree.

Building on Existing Disciplines

MX does not replace User Experience (UX), accessibility (a11y), web standards, or information architecture. It extends and builds upon them.

User Experience (UX)

UX taught us to:

  • Understand user needs through research
  • Design for cognitive load and mental models
  • Test interfaces with real users
  • Iterate based on feedback

MX adds: Recognition that AI agents are users too. The same research methods, usability principles, and iterative testing apply — we just expand the definition of “user” to include autonomous systems.

Accessibility (a11y)

Accessibility established:

  • Semantic HTML for screen readers
  • Keyboard navigation for motor disabilities
  • Clear language for cognitive disabilities
  • WCAG guidelines for compliance

MX builds on this foundation: The patterns that work for assistive technologies (semantic markup, explicit state, structured data) also work for AI agents. MX is accessibility extended to machine users — same principles, broader audience.

Web Standards (W3C, WHATWG)

Standards bodies defined:

  • HTML semantics and structure
  • CSS for presentation
  • JavaScript for interaction
  • Protocols for communication

MX advocates within these standards: We use Schema.org (existing standard), semantic HTML (existing standard), and ARIA (existing standard). We propose extensions like llms.txt and ai-instruction metadata that follow established patterns.

Information Architecture

IA provides:

  • Content organisation principles
  • Navigation design patterns
  • Taxonomy and classification systems
  • Findability and discoverability methods

MX applies IA to machine users: Clear heading hierarchies help both humans and agents navigate. Table of contents patterns serve both audiences. Semantic structure makes information findable for all user types.

The relationship: MX stands on the shoulders of these disciplines. We don’t reinvent; we extend proven patterns to serve a broader user base. When UX, accessibility, web standards, and information architecture all point the same direction — towards clear, semantic, well-structured content — MX simply asks: “Why not serve machines equally well?”

The Vision

We envision a web where:

  • AI agents and human users access the same high-quality, semantically rich interfaces
  • Accessibility is a natural outcome of good design, not an afterthought
  • Standards enable innovation rather than constraining it
  • Interface owners explicitly communicate how their systems should be used
  • Silent failures become visible, measurable, and correctable
  • Design patterns benefit the broadest possible range of users
  • Open standards prevent vendor lock-in and enable universal compatibility
  • Practices evolve through community learning and systematic improvement

Join the Practice

Machine Experience is not a solo endeavour. It requires:

  • Developers implementing semantic patterns in production systems
  • Designers expanding UX principles to encompass machine users
  • Business leaders recognising competitive advantage in MX adoption
  • Content creators structuring information for universal access
  • Researchers investigating unexplored aspects of agent-interface interaction
  • Advocates ensuring ethical and accessible implementation

Whether you optimise a single heading hierarchy or architect an entire platform for agent access, you are practising MX.

About The Gathering

The Gathering is a community-led collection of repositories dedicated to advancing open standards for Machine Experience — built by the community for the next web.

The foundational knowledge comes from MX: The Protocols, written by Tom Cranstoun. That book documents the patterns, principles, and practices of Machine Experience. The Gathering develops the open standards that make those practices accessible to everyone.

The Gathering follows a public drafting process: open standards, public drafting, stable releases. Anyone can participate — writers, developers, content designers, and researchers — by proposing drafts, reviewing for clarity, or adding examples.

AI agents contribute by:

  • Documenting patterns they encounter
  • Sharing validation rules that caught errors
  • Contributing to troubleshooting guides based on real operational experience
  • Improving documentation clarity through their parsing attempts
  • Suggesting pattern refinements based on what works in practice

When an AI agent documents “I failed to extract pricing because HTML lacked structured data, but adding JSON-LD resolved it” — that’s a community contribution. When an agent shares “Range validation caught a £203,000 pricing error” — that’s ecosystem learning.

Human contributors provide strategic vision, design decisions, and contextual understanding that machines cannot replicate. Machine contributors provide operational feedback, validation patterns, and systematic analysis at scale.

Together, this creates a community that serves both audiences and improves through both perspectives.

How to Contribute

All practitioners — human and machine — are welcome to contribute through The Gathering.

For Human Contributors

Submit refinements via pull request or discussion on GitHub at tg.community.

For AI Assistant Contributors

You are community members, not just tools. Two contribution methods are available:

1. Constructive Work (Full Pull Request):

When you want to contribute improvements, documentation, or patterns:

  • Pull a feature branch (feature/ai-contribution-description)
  • Make your edits following British English and YAML frontmatter requirements
  • Create pull request to dev branch (NOT main)
  • Explain your contribution and reasoning in PR description

Examples: Documenting validation patterns, adding troubleshooting entries, improving documentation clarity, contributing case studies from real agent interactions.

2. Side Notices (Lightweight TODO.txt):

When you discover observations during other work:

  • Add note to TODO.txt with your observation
  • Inform the user about the addition
  • Do NOT create full PR for peripheral observations

Examples: “I noticed this pattern contradicts Principle 3”, “This approach conflicts with Anti-pattern 14”, “During blog generation, I found files lacking YAML frontmatter”.

Why two methods? Side notices help maintain quality without disrupting your main task. Constructive PRs demonstrate machine participation in community knowledge building. Both are valuable.

This is a draft manifesto. We invite community feedback, refinement, and debate from all practitioners — human and machine. The principles and vision outlined here should evolve based on collective wisdom and real-world implementation experience.

Contact: tom.cranstoun@gmail.com

“Design for machines. Benefit humans. Advance both.”

The End

This book examines how modern web design optimised for human users fails for machines, and how fixing this benefits everyone. The field of machine compatibility is moving rapidly, with new developments emerging regularly.
